text: Stagecoaching in Australia

European settlers began arriving in Australia in the late 18th century. Originally, most of them stayed near the coast, where the environment was more suitable for living than further inland, but this began to change in the 19th century when the number of settlers coming as immigrants rose sharply, due to the discovery of gold in 1851. These new immigrants no longer wanted to stay near the coast; they began to move inland to the gold mining fields. This was particularly true in Victoria, where there was a sudden rise in demand for transport services as tens of thousands of people arrived in Melbourne, the main town of Victoria, and then immediately sought horse-drawn vehicles to take them to the gold fields. The main form of transport was stagecoach. These are the horse-drawn, four-wheeled vehicles which were used to transport passengers and mail and are often a feature of North American western films.

text: Prior to the discovery of gold, stagecoaches had been operating in Australia for decades. However, in Australia, stagecoach travel times were lengthy and services irregular and unreliable. This was partly because the stagecoaches were built in England and had no suspension, as they were designed to be suitable for relatively well-maintained English rural roads and city streets. They proved to be unsuitable for the rough tracks in the interior of Australia. In the rain, stagecoach services stopped altogether because the tracks became impassable due to the number of vehicles using them. During winter months, it was not uncommon for horses to stand up to their stomachs in mud and stagecoaches up to their axles, totally unable to move.

text: This, then, was the standard of stagecoach travel in Australia in 1853 when two North Americans, Freeman Cobb and George Mowton, arrived in Melbourne. They had been sent to set up an international freight service for a North American company that had greatly profited from the Californian gold rush and now hoped to profit from the Australian gold rush. However, they soon realised that demand was not for international freight but rather for the transport of people. Melbourne at the time was growing rapidly and without direction; in fact, disorder and a lack of infrastructure characterised the town. The roads were so bad that George Mowton became convinced that the difficulties of doing business in such a place outweighed any opportunity, and he returned to North America.

text: Freeman Cobb elected to stay, and together with three partners, he started Cobb & Co., a business focused on passenger stagecoach services. Stagecoach travel was necessary but notoriously uncomfortable in the imported English stagecoaches, and passengers were constantly complaining of arriving at their destinations bruised. During the journey, they suffered from motion sickness. Cobb & Co. used stagecoaches imported from North America because they were considered more suitable for Australia than English ones, having been built to withstand fast gallops on the prairie tracks of the North American mid-west, an environment similar to Australia. They were also lighter than the English stagecoaches and could travel through muddy conditions better. These stagecoaches were known as 'thoroughbrace' stagecoaches and were moderately comfortable, as for the first time they used an early form of suspension. This was in the form of leather straps from which the body of the stagecoach was suspended. Passengers found this a comfortable design as it absorbed some of the impact the wheels made on the rough roads. These more comfortable stagecoaches were popular amongst travellers, and in just a few short months, Cobb & Co. had established themselves as the preferred method of transport.

text: Cobb & Co.'s other innovations included using experienced North American stagecoach drivers, who had driven stagecoaches in California during the gold rush there. Previously, stagecoach drivers had been employed for their stamina; experience was not necessary. In addition, Cobb & Co.'s horses were not bought; they were bred by the company. In this way, the company could be certain of having horses which had the right build to ensure they were capable of pulling a fully laden stagecoach rapidly. This was a more efficient method of providing stagecoach horses than the usual approach, which had been to buy local horses that seemed fit and healthy. The company also ensured that each route was divided up into sections of around 10 to 30 miles, where staging posts were set up along the route so that teams of horses could be changed, and tired horses stabled, rested, and fed.

text: Cobb & Co. was rightly respected for its innovative approach, which set it apart from its competitors. For 70 years, from the 1850s to the 1920s, Cobb & Co. stagecoaches were a principal means of transport in the eastern half of the Australian continent.
